how-much-to-charge-for-a-metal-roof.html.text:
Metal roof bid calculator

How much to charge for a metal roof

A published “$950 a square” special prices the roof after pitch. A residential metal roof is not that number. It is a panel type that does not scale with squares, a tear-off or an overlay, one story or two, and lineal feet of ridge, hip, valley, rake, and eave the coupon never counted. Matching the coupon on a 10/12 mechanical-lock standing-seam tear-off is how a sold job becomes a week of unpaid seamer time after the first valley.

Open the free bid calculator

The number a per-square special cannot see

Take a 40×30 ranch at 4/12, 5V crimp, overlay, four pipe boots, no snow guards. That is 1,200 plan square feet, 1,264.8 roof square feet, and 12.65 squares — 13.66 panel squares after 8% waste. The coupon says about $10,750. Raise the same shop to a 50×40 two-story at 10/12. The plan is 2,000 square feet, so the coupon says about $22,130 on 26.04 squares. The job did not scale that way: mechanical-lock panels, a seamer, a full tear-off, 84 lineal feet of hip and valley, and 48 snow guards the ranch never had.

Put standing seam on that ranch. Panels now cost more per square the 5V overlay never priced. Two stories are not “the same squares plus a ladder.” A valley is not in the square number at all.

How to price it

  1. Measure building length and width.
  2. Apply the pitch: 4/12 is 1.054, 12/12 is 1.414. Roof squares are that area ÷ 100.
  3. Count panel squares after kit waste and extra waste from hips and valleys. Overlay tear-off is zero. A full tear-off covers the roof.
  4. Price panel (exposed fastener / snap-lock / mechanical-lock), stories, trim, snow guards, boots, ice-and-water, and the permit allowance.
  5. Load the wage, add materials and mobilization, mark overhead on direct cost, then divide by one minus the target margin. The walk-away price is total cost.

The metal roof bid calculator does that arithmetic in the browser from your own hours and invoices. Starting waste, hours, and material rates are ballpark figures to replace, not a catalog or a code table.

What this is not

This is not a building-code opinion, a permit, a construction specification, or an engineering stamp. Confirm the jurisdiction and a qualified professional before sending a price. The output is arithmetic on the numbers you typed.

No warranty. This free article and calculator are not construction, legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from their use. Common questions

How much to charge for a metal roof?

Start from the building plan, apply the pitch to get roof squares, then count panel squares after waste, tear-off, stories, trim, snow guards, and the permit. A published $950 per square special only sees roof squares after pitch.

Why do standing seam and a tear-off change the price?

A 40-by-30 ranch at 4/12 is 12.65 squares of 5V overlay. A 50-by-40 two-story at 10/12 is 26.04 squares of mechanical-lock standing seam, a full tear-off, valleys, and snow guards. Matching the ranch coupon is how the standing-seam job loses money.

Is this a building-code calculation?

No. Pitch multipliers, waste, and panel rates here are common starting points on residential bids. They are not a building-code opinion, a permit, or an engineering stamp.

Where the hours go

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting pitches, waste, hours, and material rates are common ballpark figures, not a building-code opinion, a permit, a warranty, or an engineering stamp. Time your own crews and replace them.

    Common questions

    Why can a competitor advertise $950 a square for a metal roof?

    Usually because the special is written around one specific job, and that job is a preset here: a 40 × 30 ranch at 4/12, exposed-fastener 5V panels laid straight over the existing shingles, one storey, no valleys, no snow guards. It really does price low. What the per-square number cannot see is panel type, pitch, tear-off, stories, trim lineal feet, ice-and-water, and snow guards. Price your actual roof beside the special and the gap becomes a list of line items you can show the homeowner instead of an argument about who is honest.

    How is standing seam different from exposed fastener in the price?

    They are different products and different labor. Exposed-fastener panels (5V, R-panel, corrugated) screw through the face and go on fastest. Snap-lock standing seam costs more in panel and takes longer. Mechanical-lock standing seam is the most of both — it needs a seamer run over every seam, which is time nothing in a per-square number accounts for. Choosing the panel here changes material and hours together, because in the field they never move separately.

    Does pitch change the price the same way it does on a shingle roof?

    The geometry is the same — more pitch, more surface for the same footprint, and slower work on it — but the exposure is worse on metal, because a steeper roof usually also means more valley and more trim, and both are priced by the lineal foot here rather than by the square. That is the practical difference: on shingles a steep roof is mostly more squares; on metal it is more squares and a longer cut list.

    Is it cheaper to lay metal over the existing shingles?

    On the bid, yes, and the calculator will show you exactly how much: an overlay skips tear-off labor and the disposal that goes with it. Whether it is allowed is a separate question this tool does not answer — layer limits, deck condition, and underlayment requirements are set by your jurisdiction and the panel manufacturer, and nothing here is a code opinion, a permit, or a warranty determination. Price both and take the decision to the inspector, not to the spreadsheet.

    Why are ridge, hip, valley, rake, and eave entered separately?

    Because trim is bought and installed by the lineal foot, and a roof with the same square count can have wildly different trim runs. A simple gable has ridge, rake, and eave and nothing else; a hip roof with two valleys and a dormer has all five, and the cut, flash, and seal time is where a metal job's hours actually go. Boots and snow guards are counted per unit for the same reason.

    Why isn't a 20% margin the same as adding 20% to my cost?

    Margin here is a share of the final price — price = job cost ÷ (1 − margin) — which is how the quote reads to the homeowner and how your books read it. Overhead is a separate markup on direct cost, applied before margin and never to itself or to profit. A $22,000 cost marked up 20% is $26,400, a 16.7% margin; a 20% target margin is $27,500. vs-a-flat-950-per-square-special.html.text:
← Metal Roof Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $950/square metal-roof special

"$950 a square" is not a price for a metal-roof install -- it is a price for one specific panel, pitch, and scope, quietly applied to every roof the truck pulls up to.

What a flat $950/square special is

A flat per-square special is the fastest way to quote: one coupon number, easy to advertise and easy for a homeowner to compare between roofers. It is the number a homeowner holding a competitor's flyer will call and ask a shop to match, whatever roof is actually up there.

The number behind it was set for one job -- a low-pitch overlay over existing shingles, one story, an easy exposed-fastener panel, and minimal trim -- and then reused for every roof afterward, whether or not the next job looks anything like the ranch overlay it was priced on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the plan dimensions and pitch, the panel type -- exposed fastener, snap-lock, or mechanical-lock standing seam -- overlay or full tear-off, stories, trim lineal feet by run, snow guards, pipe boots, and ice-and-water, plus your loaded labor and overhead. It prices the panel, the tear-off, the stories, and every trim run separately, and returns a walk-away price below which the job loses money -- for this roof, not a generic one.

What a flat $950/square special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same per-square number whether the job is a 5V overlay on a 4/12 ranch or a mechanical-lock standing-seam tear-off on a 10/12 two-story with valleys and snow guards. Prices the panel, pitch, and scope from what was entered, so the two jobs above come out at different numbers instead of one.
Has no line for a tear-off, so stripping a roof to deck gets quoted the same as a job that only ever needed an overlay. Adds tear-off hours and a dumpster fee per square only when a full tear-off is entered, so the strip shows up instead of being absorbed.
Has no line for a portable seamer, so a mechanical-lock standing seam gets quoted the same as an easy exposed-fastener panel. Adds seamer hours and a seamer fee only for a mechanical-lock panel, so the lock-forming machine costs more than a screw gun.
Assumes one story and minimal trim, so a two-story roof or a run of ridge, hip, valley, rake, and eave gets quoted the same as a simple ranch. Prices extra story hours and every trim run by its own lineal feet, so a roof with hips and valleys costs more than one without.
Gives the crew a coupon price to quote, not a number to check a quote against when a homeowner asks to match a cheaper overlay special on a tear-off job. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against the flat special, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the crew commits to it.

Three roofs, the same per-square special

Using this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($36/hr crew wage, 32% payroll burden, 15% overhead on direct cost, a 25% target margin, $160 travel and equipment):

JobThis calculator's break-even costThe flat $950/square specialVerdict
12.65 squares, 5V overlay, 4/12 ranch, one story -- the job the $950/square special is built on$8,322.86$12,015.60Covers, +$3,692.74
18.46 squares, 5V tear-off, 8/12 Cape, two stories$14,471.00$17,539.58Loses $3,068.59 below break-even once a tear-off and a second story enter
26.04 squares, mechanical-lock standing seam tear-off, 10/12 two-story, valleys, snow guards$35,050.90$24,738.00Loses $10,312.90 below break-even

The flat special is $950 times the roof's own squares, not derived from any of the three jobs' scope. It covers the ranch overlay it was written for with room to spare, then falls further behind as tear-off, stories, and a mechanical-lock panel stack up -- exactly the jobs a flat per-square rate cannot see. Run your own roof's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat special is not wrong because it is simple -- it is wrong when it is applied outside the one roof it was built for, and nothing about a per-square coupon tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat special skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat $950/square metal-roof special get a bid wrong?

Because the cost driver is panel type, tear-off, stories, and trim, not "roof squares" alone. A 12-square 5V-crimp overlay on a 4/12 ranch is a different job from a 26-square mechanical-lock standing-seam tear-off on a 10/12 two-story with valleys and snow guards -- and a flat per-square number cannot see which one it is looking at.

What does a flat per-square special usually leave out entirely?

The tear-off, the seamer time for a mechanical-lock standing seam, the story premium, the trim lineal feet, ice-and-water, and snow guards. A published per-square special is priced on the overlay -- panel over existing shingles, no tear-off, one story, minimal trim -- and has nowhere to put the hours for stripping a roof to deck, running a portable seamer, working a steep two-story, or every foot of ridge, hip, valley, rake, and eave.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($36/hr crew wage, 32% burden, 15% overhead, a 25% target margin, $160 travel and equipment): a 12.65-square 5V overlay on a 4/12 ranch -- the job the $950/square special is built on -- breaks even at $8,322.86 against the special's $12,015.60, so the special actually covers this job with $3,692.74 to spare. An 18.46-square 5V tear-off on an 8/12 two-story Cape breaks even at $14,471.00 against the special's $17,539.58 -- still short by $3,068.59 once a tear-off and a second story enter the bid. A 26.04-square mechanical-lock standing-seam tear-off on a 10/12 two-story with valleys and snow guards breaks even at $35,050.90 against the special's $24,738.00, over $10,300 below break-even.

Is a flat per-square special ever the right way to quote a metal roof?

For the one job it was actually priced on -- a low-pitch overlay, one story, an easy panel, minimal trim -- a flat rate can land close, and on this calculator's own numbers it does, with room to spare. The risk is applying it to a tear-off, a steeper pitch, extra stories, or a mechanical-lock standing seam without noticing, because the coupon does not know which roof it is looking at and neither does the crew until the tear-off starts.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local labor or material rates. It takes the plan dimensions, pitch, panel type, tear-off, stories, trim lineal feet, snow guards, ice-and-water, and your loaded labor and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price for the roof you describe -- the arithmetic a flat special skips, not a market survey.

This calculator vs. AccuLynx

Two different shapes: AccuLynx is an account-based platform for running a roofing company's whole sales-to-production pipeline. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one metal-roof job cost, given its panel type, tear-off, stories, and trim, before you send the bid.

What each tool is for

AccuLynx is a cloud-based business management platform built specifically for roofing contractors, headquartered in Beloit, Wisconsin. It is built around running a roofing company's whole pipeline in one account: lead capture and CRM, aerial roof measurement, estimating and proposal generation, material ordering with supplier integrations, production and crew scheduling, and job costing, used by a sales team, a production manager, and office staff together across every job the company runs, on an ongoing subscription. It is a large enough business in that niche that in July 2025 Verisk Analytics — the NYSE-listed insurance-data and analytics company — signed a definitive agreement to acquire it in an all-cash deal valued at $2.35 billion, a deal a Delaware Chancery Court later ordered Verisk to complete after a dispute over its regulatory review. AccuLynx's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity, category, and the acquisition — reported by Verisk's own newsroom and multiple trade and financial press outlets — are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no subscription price for it appears on this page.

This calculator does none of that. It does not track a lead, order material, schedule a crew, or hold a record across jobs. It takes one metal-roof job — panel type (exposed-fastener 5V/R-panel/corrugated, snap-lock standing seam, or mechanical-lock standing seam), the building's length, width, and pitch converted to pitch-adjusted panel squares, waste, whether it is an overlay or a full tear-off, stories, ridge, hip, valley, rake, and eave trim by the lineal foot, snow guards, pipe boots, ice-and-water shield, loaded labor, mobilization, dumpster, permit, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep — and turns that into the job price, the price per square, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, plus a printable customer proposal with a deposit split and a price-held date. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
